title: [Autour de La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois, pages 1 à 67] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. Y is a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field k (the curve case of an 'anabelian elementary Artin variety'). Ŷ is its smooth completion, I = Ŷ \ Y, and J_Y is the generalized Jacobian of Y with reduced modulus I. J^0_Y is the Picard group of the 'pinched' curve Y' obtained from Ŷ by contracting I to one point. It is an extension of J^0_Ŷ by the torus G_m^I/G_m. Y embeds in the torsor J^1_Y.

Lemma (previous page). Let u ∈ J^0_Y(k) and let U ⊂ Y be a nonempty open set with U+u ⊂ Y. Then u = 0 (written multiplicatively as u = 1).

Previous page, complete case. If u ≠ 0, translation T_u restricted to Ŷ is a fixed-point-free automorphism. It acts trivially on H^1 because H^1(J) ≅ H^1(Ŷ), so its Lefschetz number is 2−2g. That is a contradiction unless g = 1.

This page, torus case. Assume u lies in the toric part, so u is given by (λ_i)_{i∈I}, λ_i ∈ k*, modulo the diagonal.
- Concretely, u is the trivial line bundle on Ŷ whose fibres at the points ŷ_i ∈ I are glued to one another via the λ_i, giving a line bundle on Y'.
- Then u+x (x ∈ Y) is represented by O_Ŷ(x) with these gluings.
- For u+x = y with y ∈ Y, the two must first have the same image in J^1_Ŷ.
- For g ≥ 1, Abel–Jacobi Ŷ → J^1_Ŷ is injective, so x = y. Comparing the gluing data then forces λ to be diagonal, i.e. u = 0.
- For g = 0, the anabelian hypothesis gives card I ≥ 3. Grothendieck picks J ⊂ I with two elements and replaces Ŷ by the curve Ŷ_J pinched at J. Its J^1 is a G_m-torsor and P^1 \ J ≅ G_m maps isomorphically to it. From this he concludes x = y, so u = 0.

Bracketed remark. For u ∈ Ker(J^0_Y → J^0_Ŷ) one has (Y+u) ∩ Y = ∅ unless u = 0. If U+u ⊂ Y, then u lies in that kernel, since the induced endomorphism of Ŷ is translation by ū and the complete case applies. Hence u = 0. Grothendieck notes these arguments only work for g ≠ 1; the margin asks 'g ≥ 2?'.

Why g = 1 is special. When Ŷ is an elliptic curve, ū can be a nonzero translation preserving Ŷ. The margin records this: 'Curiously, one does not get that the image of u in J_Ŷ is zero!'.

Next step. He therefore switches to a cohomological argument. Consider the two maps i, j: U → Y. Since translations act trivially on H_1 and H_1(Y) ≅ H_1(J_Y), one gets H_1(i) = H_1(j). He then analyses the kernels of H_1(U) → H_1(Y), generated by the parabolic (inertia) subgroups L_j, to show that the completed map f fixes I and is the identity.

Purpose. This is a 'geometric proof' of Th. 2 cor. 1 b), a rigidity statement for anabelian elementary Artin neighbourhoods inside the Longue Marche project (automorphisms or endomorphisms detected by π_1).
errors: The g = 0 step is incomplete as written. Using a single two-element J ⊂ I, the condition 'same image in J^1_{Ŷ_J}' only gives y = λ_J·x in a coordinate on P^1 \ J ≅ G_m, where λ_J is the image of u. It does not give x = y. One needs at least two different pairs, e.g. {0,∞} and {1,∞}: y = λx and y−1 = μ(x−1) for all x in U force λ = μ = 1. Equivalently, u+x = y with x ≠ y must be excluded using all coordinates of the torus. The gap is easily filled.

On the previous page, the claim 'U+u ⊂ Y implies the image of u in the abelian part is zero' fails for g = 1, where translation by a point preserves an elliptic curve. Grothendieck himself notices this in the margin and in the bracket ('ces arguments ne marchent que pour g ≠ 1').
Minor: in the bracket, the kernel used should be Ker(J^0_Y → J^0_Ŷ), and the conclusion should read u = 0 (multiplicatively u = 1). The notation switches between additive and multiplicative.

ideas.what: Description of the generalized Jacobian of an affine curve with reduced modulus as Pic^0 of the curve pinched at the boundary. It is an extension of Jac(Ŷ) by G_m^I/G_m, with torus coordinates given by gluing of fibres of line bundles.
ideas.modern_name: Rosenlicht–Serre generalized Jacobian (modulus m = Σ_{i∈I} P_i)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Rosenlicht (1954), Serre (Groupes algébriques et corps de classes, 1959)
ideas.where_published: Standard (Serre, GACC); Grothendieck uses it routinely, e.g. 1-motives / SGA 7 context

ideas.what: A nontrivial translation of the Jacobian cannot preserve a curve of genus ≠ 1, shown via the Lefschetz fixed-point formula (Lefschetz number 2−2g).
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz fixed point argument / rigidity of the Abel–Jacobi embedding

ideas.what: Lemma: if a generic translate U+u of a hyperbolic affine curve lies in the curve inside its generalized Jacobian, then u = 0. Proved by dévissage from elementary Artin neighbourhoods to curves, with a separate cohomological (H_1, parabolic subgroups) argument to cover genus 1.
ideas.modern_name: rigidity of hyperbolic curves in their generalized Albanese; translation-invariance / finiteness of automorphisms of hyperbolic curves
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore; related statements for Albanese of hyperbolic varieties
ideas.where_published: Only in these unpublished Longue Marche notes as far as I know

ideas.what: Using partial pinchings Ŷ_J (J ⊂ I with two elements) to separate points on P^1 minus ≥3 points via quotients G_m of the toric part.
ideas.modern_name: projection of the generalized Jacobian onto quotients of the toric part (cross-ratio type coordinates)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine auxiliary lemma in a rigidity argument for anabelian elementary Artin neighbourhoods: generic translates of a hyperbolic curve inside its generalized Jacobian are trivial. The mathematics is classical (generalized Jacobians, Lefschetz, Abel–Jacobi injectivity). It contains a small fixable gap in the g = 0 case, and Grothendieck's own recognition that genus 1 needs a cohomological treatment. Nothing new to specialists.
transcription_corrections: 'Y' = Ŷ_{∐_I}' is more plausibly 'Y' = Ŷ_I' (the curve deduced from Ŷ by contracting I to a point).
': k par les ∂_i' should likely read '≃ k par les λ_i' (the λ_i ∈ k* introduced on the previous page).
'Pour que x [?] soit de la forme y' should read 'Pour que u+x soit de la forme y (y ∈ Y)'.
The inserted phrase is closer to 'et comme Ŷ se plonge dans J^1_Ŷ' (Abel–Jacobi embedding), placed with '(pour un g ≥ 1)'.
'u ∈ Ker(J_Y → J_Ŷ)' is likely 'u ∈ Ker(J^0_Y → J^0_Ŷ)'.
'(donc = 1)' is in multiplicative notation and means u = 0 / u trivial.
Margin: 'Curieusement on n'a pas que l'image de u dans J^0_Ŷ est nulle !'
